meta.title: OSMI Mental Health in Tech Survey

config.description: OSMI Mental Health in Tech Survey 2017+2018 combined — tech workers on workplace mental health

questions.Q_EC: Describe the conversation you had with your employer about your mental health, including their reactions and what actions were taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
questions.Q_CC: Describe the conversation with coworkers you had about your mental health including their reactions.
questions.Q_CW: Describe the conversation your coworker had with you about their mental health (please do not use names).
questions.Q_PE: Describe the conversation you had with your previous employer about your mental health, including their reactions and actions taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
questions.Q_PC: Describe the conversation you had with your previous coworkers about your mental health including their reactions.
questions.Q_CA: How has being identified as a person with a mental health issue affected your career?
questions.Q_BH: Describe the circumstances of the badly handled or unsupportive response.
questions.Q_SH: Describe the circumstances of the supportive or well handled response.
questions.Q_ID: Briefly describe what you think the industry as a whole and/or employers could do to improve mental health support for employees.
questions.Q_AE: If there is anything else you would like to tell us that has not been covered by the survey questions, please use this space to do so.

Q_EC.human: I had to take a personal day to deal with stress and grief. It wasn't following anything in particular, so I felt a little awkward but she was very understanding and urged me to take the time I needed.

variants.t: I told my manager I was struggling with burnout and needed some time off. He was very understanding and told me to take the week. We also discussed adjusting my deadlines once I got back to office work.

I asked for a private meeting, explained I was feeling burnt out and anxious, and requested flexible hours. My manager listened, expressed concern, offered a temporary reduced schedule, and arranged a referral to our employee assistance program.

I spoke with my supervisor about my ongoing anxiety issues during our weekly check-in. He was surprisingly supportive and suggested I work from home two days a week to help manage my stress levels, which has been very helpful.

I scheduled a private meeting, explained I’d been feeling exhausted and anxious, and asked for flexibility. My manager listened, expressed concern, offered a reduced workload for two weeks, and suggested I use the company’s mental‑health counseling service.

I talked to my manager about my PTSD after a really rough week. She was super supportive -- we sat down and figured out a flexible schedule so I could attend therapy without feeling guilty about my deadlines. It helped a lot.

I sat down with my manager after a rough week, explained my anxiety and PTSD triggers, and he listened without judgment. He arranged a flexible schedule, offered an employee‑assistance session, and checked in weekly to see how I was coping.

I sat down with my lead when things got HEAVY with my PTSD. I was honest about needing space and he was honestly great—no prying, just "what do you need?" We pushed some project milestones back so I could focus on recovery without the constant pressure. It made a huge difference tbh

I sat down with my manager after a rough week, told them Ive been dealing with anxiety and PTSD triggers, and asked for some flexibility. honestly they were SUPPORTIVE—actually offered a reduced workload, weekly check ins, and pointed me to the company’s employee assistance program, though I still worry about stigma

My manager was actually pretty receptive — I'd caught her at a good moment, I think. I told her I was dealing with some ongoing anxiety and PTSD stuff that was making certain crunch periods really hard. She didn't push for details, which I appreciated. We agreed I could flex my hours during heavy deadlines and check in with her if things got bad. It wasn't a formal accommodation, more like a quiet understanding between us -- honestly that felt safer than going through HR.

I talked to my creative director after a pretty rough stretch -- grief and a PTSD flare hitting at the same time. She was genuinely good about it, honestly. We scaled back my deadline load for a few weeks and she checked in without making it weird. Not every workplace handles that well, so I was relieved

I talked to my direct manager when the PTSD was making it hard to focus — she was genuinely good about it, no weird energy. We agreed on a lighter meeting load for a few weeks and she checked in without making it a thing. Honestly, that mattered more than any formal policy.

I've talked to my manager a few times -- around grief and then later when the anxiety was getting unmanageable. Both times they were genuinely receptive, which honestly surprised me a little. We adjusted deadlines and I got a few days to decompress. Not every workplace would do that, so I know I'm lucky.

Q_CC.human: This is hard because there are some coworkers that are VERY easy to talk to, and it's no big deal to talk about anxiety, depression, whatever. Others are more standoffish and not as emotionally available.  I would only discuss it with them if it impacted my work, and in the context of what I was doing to get better.

variants.t: I told my team I was struggling with anxiety during a project. They were supportive and told me to rest up.
I mentioned to a couple of close colleagues that I was feeling overwhelmed and taking a break. They were supportive and offered to cover my tasks.
I mentioned feeling overwhelmed during lunch; a few coworkers nodded, one suggested taking short breaks, and another offered to cover a task temporarily.
I told a few close colleagues that I was struggling with anxiety. They were very understanding and shared some of their own personal experiences too.
I mentioned feeling overwhelmed during lunch; a few coworkers nodded, one offered to share tasks, another suggested taking short walks together for breaks.
honestly, I’ve mentioned my anxiety and grief to my team. They were incredibly empathetic -- most of them have their own stuff going on too. it felt safe
I brought it up during lunch; a few nodded, one said “I get it,” another offered to cover my deadlines, and we all agreed to check in regularly.

My core team is AMAZING. I’ve been pretty open about my anxiety and grief with them—they’re super supportive and it’s honestly just how we operate. Most of them just listened or shared their own stuff. It made me feel way less alone in the studio tbh

I opened up to a small group of teammates after a particularly intense project deadline. Most of them responded with genuine concern—one said, “Take whatever time you need,” another shared their own anxiety struggles. Their support helped me feel less isolated, though I still worry about being seen as fragile

My team is pretty unusual in that we actually talk about this stuff. A couple of colleagues have their own anxiety and depression stuff going on, so it's kind of normalized in our group. I mentioned the PTSD piece to two people I'm close with -- their reaction was just... matter-of-fact, supportive. No weirdness. That's not something I take for granted.

My closest coworkers already knew -- we're pretty open with each other about that stuff, which honestly makes a huge difference. A few of them have their own anxiety or depression stuff going on, so it landed without the awkwardness you'd get elsewhere. They just kind of rallied, checked in, brought snacks. It felt like community, not crisis management.

Most of my close coworkers already knew -- we talk about this stuff pretty openly in our team. no formal "conversation," it just comes up naturally. A few people shared their own stuff back, which honestly made it easier.

Most of my coworkers already know -- we've built that kind of culture deliberately. I've mentioned the PTSD and anxiety to a few people and mostly gotten warmth back. One colleague shared their own stuff in return, which made it feel less like disclosure and more like just... talking. There's one or two people I wouldn't go there with, but that's just reading the room.

Q_CW.human: I have a handful of close friends at work. As creatives, I think it's a given that we all struggle with deep insecurity and depression to some extent. As far as I'm concerned, there's very little stigma - it's almost a given.

variants.t: A close colleague of mine pulled me aside during a lunch break a few months ago. They admitted they had been struggling significantly with clinical depression for a while and were finding it hard to stay motivated with our current sprint goals. I just listened mostly and told them I appreciated them trusting me with that information. We talked about how the pressure in tech can be overwhelming sometimes. I suggested they take some time off if the company benefits allowed for it.
A colleague once told me they were dealing with severe anxiety and were starting therapy. I listened and told them I appreciated them sharing. We talked about how the project stress was a factor.

They whispered that they’d been struggling with anxiety after a recent project deadline, explained feeling constantly exhausted, and asked if I could help review their code. I listened, reassured them, and suggested taking a short break together.
A teammate recently pulled me aside to mention they were feeling burnt out and overwhelmed. We talked about setting better boundaries with our project deadlines to help lower their stress.

During a quick coffee break, my teammate confessed feeling burnt out after recent project deadlines, described persistent anxiety, and asked if I’d share coping strategies; I listened, offered support, and suggested using our employee assistance program.
A close friend at work opened up about their depression and burnout. we talked for a while and i shared my own experiences with grief -- they seemed really relieved to just finally be heard

My teammate confided that they’ve been battling severe anxiety and occasional panic attacks after a recent project failure; they said they felt isolated, asked for flexible deadlines, and appreciated my promise to listen and help whenever needed.

One of my peers opened up about their burnout during a late-night push. they were SUPER stressed about letting the team down—classic creative guilt. I just listened and told them it’s okay to be human. It felt good to be that safe space for them ngl

A teammate pulled me aside after a sprint review and admitted they’ve been battling depression and feeling burnt out. they sounded pretty raw, and I told them I get it—tbh I’ve dealt with anxiety myself. we talked about using the companys counseling service and agreed to check in weekly

One of my closer colleagues opened up about burnout and some really heavy grief stuff — they'd lost someone and it was colliding with a brutal project timeline. They came to me first, I think, because they knew I'd get it. I just listened mostly, didn't try to fix anything. We ended up talking for a while and I checked in with them over the following weeks. That kind of conversation feels like what a team should be, honestly.

They came to me during a really low stretch -- mentioned they were struggling with burnout and some stuff from home bleeding into everything. I didn't push or try to fix it, just listened and shared a bit of my own experience so they knew they weren't alone. Honestly that kind of reciprocal thing is what makes our team feel different from places I've worked before.

One of my closest collaborators told me they'd been dealing with pretty severe anxiety — like, functioning but barely. they came to me specifically because they knew I'd been open about my own stuff. I just listened, didn't try to fix it. that's usually what people need first.

It's happened a few times. The most recent was a colleague who came to me during a rough patch -- talked about burnout and some family stuff they were carrying. I mostly just listened. They didn't need solutions, they needed to feel heard, and I think that's something our team has gotten genuinely good at creating space for.

It’s really hard to find a company that actually walks the walk when it comes to mental health. Even though my current boss is great, I still feel a bit nervous about being fully open because of how my last job went. We need more transparency everywhere.

Honestly, I just think it’s vital to remember that in creative tech, our brains ARE the product. If we’re struggling with things like PTSD or anxiety, the work just isnt going to be there. Supporting us isn't some corporate favor—it’s just good business. I’m glad someone is actually ASKING these questions tbh

Honestly tbh, I dont think any single policy will fix everything—what matters is a culture where we can talk about grief, anxiety, or PTSD without feeling judged. i'd love to see regular peer‑support circles and managers trained to recognise subtle signs, not just crises

Just that I hope this data actually goes somewhere. Surveys like this can feel like shouting into a void — you share real stuff and then wonder if it's just going to sit in a spreadsheet. The issues aren't mysterious. People in positions of power either prioritize this or they don't, and employees figure that out pretty fast. I'm lucky to be somewhere it's taken seriously now. Not everyone gets that, and I think about that a lot.
Not much to add — I think the questions covered the important ground. I'd just say the manager relationship is really the crux of all of it.
I mentioned my panic attacks to my old manager. He seemed confused and suggested I try to manage my time better.

My last boss was okay but definitely more awkward than my current lead. I mentioned my anxiety during a review and they sort of just nodded and said "take some time if you need it." There wasn't really a plan--so I just kept my head down and worked through it. It felt a bit DISMISSIVE tbh

I met with my former manager after a particularly stressful quarter, told them Ive been coping with anxiety and occasional PTSD flashbacks and asked if we could adjust my deadlines. honestly they were surprisingly supportive—offered flexible hours, a temporary reduced load, and connected me to their EAP, which helped a lot. it felt like a relief

The culture was so different — night and day compared to where I am now. I brought up some anxiety stuff during a one-on-one and my manager kind of just... nodded and moved on. Nothing happened. No follow-up, no adjustments. I got the sense it was treated as a personal problem I needed to sort out on my own time. I didn't bring it up again after that.

It wasn't as smooth as things are now, honestly. I disclosed some anxiety stuff to a manager at a previous job -- more out of necessity than comfort, because it was affecting my output visibly. She was sympathetic in the moment but nothing really changed structurally. I got a vague "let me know if you need anything" and that was kind of it. No follow-through, no adjusted workload, just... the bare minimum of acknowledgment before we both moved on.

Very different vibe from my current job. My previous manager got kind of awkward and defaulted to HR, which honestly felt like being handed off rather than supported. Nothing concrete came of it -- they sent me a list of EAP resources and that was basically it.

Very different dynamic. My previous employer wasn't bad exactly, but the culture was more traditional -- HR kind of culture where you'd file a thing and hope for the best. I mentioned burnout once and got pointed to an EAP that I never ended up using. Functional but cold, I guess.
I only mentioned my stress to a couple of desk mates once. They didn't really know what to say, so we just went back to work.
I kept it mostly to myself at my old company. I only mentioned my depression once to a teammate who seemed to be struggling too.
I shared feeling chronically stressed; a few colleagues offered empathy, one suggested therapy, and another promised to help with upcoming deadlines.
I mentioned my stress levels to a few people, but we never really discussed it deeply.
I told them I was anxious; they offered empathy, suggested breaks, and shared personal coping tips.
i mentioned my ptsd to some work friends at my last company. they were actually really cool and kept things low-key--it was supportive
I told my former team I was dealing with anxiety and grief; they responded with empathy, offered to adjust workloads, and checked in regularly.

I was pretty vocal with my desk mates at the old studio. When my grief was hitting hard, I just told them I might be "off" for a bit and they were honestly GREAT—brought me coffee, let me vent... it was a really supportive little bubble in a high-stress environment tbh

I told a few of my old teammates that Ive been dealing with anxiety and some PTSD flashbacks after that big product launch. they were really caring—one said 'take the time you need', another shared their own burnout story. tbh it helped, but I still feel a bit uneasy about how it'll affect future projects

It was more surface-level than what I have now. People were friendly enough, but nobody really went there — mental health wasn't something that came up unless someone was visibly falling apart. I mentioned being stressed a couple times and got the usual "yeah, same" kind of response. Commiseration but not connection, if that makes sense. I didn't push it further because it was pretty clear the culture wasn't set up for that kind of openness.

Most of them didn't really know -- I kept it pretty contained at that job, partly because the culture wasn't there and partly because I'd learned to read the room. There was one person I trusted enough to say something to, and she was kind, but also kind of at a loss for what to do with it. We didn't really have a shared language for that stuff the way I do with my current team. It just kind of sat there between us and we moved on.

It varied a lot. Some were great — same kind of openness I have now. But a few got uncomfortable and kind of changed the subject, which you learn to read pretty fast. Nothing hostile, just... not somewhere they were ready to go.

Mixed bag, honestly. A couple of people were great -- one in particular checked in on me after I'd mentioned being burned out, which I didn't expect. Others kind of went quiet, like they weren't sure what to do with it. It wasn't hostile, just... not the culture I have now. People were friendly but not really equipped for that kind of openness.
After I told him about the panic attacks, he didn't offer any accommodations. Instead, he just assigned me more tasks to keep me busy, which made my anxiety much worse.

I worked with a lead who treated my PTSD like a technical bug. Whenever I needed a mental health day, they’d ask "when will this be fixed?" It was honestly DEHUMANIZING—it felt like my value was only tied to my output. definitely the main reason I left that studio tbh

When I finally told my manager about my PTSD flare‑ups, they brushed it off, saying “just push through” and even cut my project deadline without offering any SUPPORT. I dont think that was ok, though later HR stepped in and gave me resources

It was a one-on-one that I'd actually prepared for — I'd thought about what I wanted to say, kept it professional, framed it around work impact rather than just venting. My manager listened, nodded, and then literally moved on to the next agenda item. That was it. No follow-up email, no "let me look into what we can do," nothing. A few weeks later he mentioned offhand that I seemed "a bit distracted lately" -- like the conversation had never happened. That erasure, honestly, was worse than if he'd just said he didn't know how to help.

The previous job situation -- I'd been visibly struggling to meet deadlines and finally said something to my manager because I felt like I had no other option. She listened, said the right things in the moment, but the conversation basically ended there. No check-in the following week, no adjusted expectations, nothing. And then over the next month or so I just... noticed I was getting cc'd less, left off meeting invites I'd normally be on. Nobody said anything. It was all very polite and very useless.

The previous job situation is the clearest example. I'd gone to my manager during a genuinely rough stretch — grief on top of existing anxiety, not functioning great — and instead of just... talking to me, she immediately said she'd "loop in HR to make sure I was supported properly." which felt clinical in a way that stung. HR sent a PDF. An actual PDF. I never heard from my manager about it again.

The EAP thing at my previous job was the clearest example. I flagged burnout to my manager -- not dramatically, just honestly -- and the response was essentially "have you looked into our employee assistance program?" with a pamphlet link. No follow-up, no real acknowledgment. It wasn't cruel, but it was a way of closing the door while technically keeping it open, and I knew not to bring it up again after that.
My current lead noticed I was burnt out and told me to take a long weekend. He didn't ask for details but made sure my tickets were covered while I was out.
My boss was understanding.
Manager offered flexible schedule
Manager allowed remote work.
Manager gave flexible schedule.
Flexible hours for therapy
Flexible schedule, weekly check‑ins

My current lead really stepped up when things got heavy. he didn't pry or act weird—he just asked "what do you need?" and we actually adjusted my milestones. It was such a HUGE relief to be treated like a human being instead of just a resource. It made staying at the studio an easy choice tbh

I sat down with my manager after a tough sprint and told them about my PTSD triggers—honestly they listened, offered flexible hours, set up regular check‑ins and connected me with the company’s counseling program. it felt really supportive tbh gave me space to heal

My current manager — that conversation I described earlier. What made it land was that she actually paused. Like, she closed her laptop. I'd kind of braced for another nod-and-move-on situation, so that small thing registered. She asked one or two questions — not prying, just enough to show she was actually tracking what I was saying. And then she followed through, which is the part that matters most to me now. The flex hours thing actually happened. I didn't have to remind her or advocate twice.

My current creative director -- that situation I mentioned. I came to her during a genuinely hard stretch and she didn't just absorb the information and move on. She actually did something. Reduced my deadline load, checked in the following week, and did it in a way that felt like a colleague rather than HR going through a checklist. What made it feel well-handled was that she followed through without me having to ask again -- which is honestly a low bar, but it's one a lot of managers don't clear.

The current job, same situation I mentioned — going to my manager about the PTSD. What made it work was that she didn't treat it like a problem to route somewhere else. She just... talked to me. Asked what would actually help, made a couple of concrete adjustments, and then followed up a week later like a normal person. No forms, no referrals, no PDF. just a human response to a human thing.

The conversation with my current manager when the anxiety peaked -- that one stands out. I came in not really knowing what I needed, and instead of defaulting to process, she just... asked questions. Listened first. Then we problem-solved together, which felt like being treated as a person rather than a liability. That's a harder thing to manufacture than most employers realize.
Providing better insurance for therapy and training managers to handle burnout would make a huge difference.

industry-wide, we need to stop treating mental health like a PR checkbox. It’s about the CULTURE—studios need to normalize vulnerability and actually back it up with realistic workloads. Managers should be trained to listen instead of just "fixing" people like they're broken code. It’s honestly about seeing the human first tbh

I think the industry should make mental‑health resources a core benefit, not an afterthought—regular, confidential check‑ins, flexible work options, and clear anti‑stigma training for all levels, tbh employers also need to empower teams to share experiences without fear of career repercussions

The biggest thing is making it normal BEFORE someone's in crisis. Managers who only respond when someone's visibly breaking down aren't support systems — they're triage. Training helps, but culture is set from the top, and it shows in small moments. And honestly, follow-through matters more than any policy document or EAP link in a company handbook.

Normalize follow-through as the actual standard -- not just having the conversation, but doing something after it. "Let me know if you need anything" is not support, it's a door closing politely. Managers need training on what comes NEXT, not just how to listen in the moment. And honestly, the industry needs to stop treating mental health as an HR checkbox and start building it into how teams are actually structured and evaluated.

Train managers to actually sit with these conversations instead of routing immediately to HR. That reflex — "let me loop in the right people" — is a liability response dressed up as support, and employees can feel the difference. The industry could do more to build psychological safety at the team level, because honestly, top-down wellness initiatives mostly feel performative. What actually works is a manager who treats it like a human problem, not a process.

Stop treating mental health support as a liability management exercise -- that's the core thing. EAPs and pamphlets exist to cover the company, not the employee, and most people can tell the difference. What actually works is managers who are trained to just LISTEN before they redirect, and cultures where disclosure doesn't feel like a career calculation. The industry tends to confuse policy with culture, and they're not the same thing at all.

It’s been a double-edged sword. In my immediate circle, being open has actually STRENGTHENED my work—vulnerability is a huge part of the creative process anyway. But I’m definitely more selective about new roles now. I won't work for a studio that treats mental health like a liability tbh

Being known as someone who deals with anxiety and PTSD has been a double‑edged sword. some managers gave me flexibility and trusted me with creative projects, but others hesitated to assign high‑visibility work, fearing I might need accommodations, kinda limiting some growth tbh

Honestly, it's hard to separate out cleanly. At my current job I don't think it's hurt me -- if anything, being someone who talks about this stuff openly has made me more approachable to colleagues dealing with their own things. At my previous place though... I suspect it quietly cost me some credibility, even if nothing overt happened. I'll never really know for sure.

Honestly, it's been mixed. At my current place, I don't think it's hurt me — if anything, being open about it has made me a more trusted colleague somehow. But at the previous job I'm less sure. Nothing was ever said directly, but I noticed I stopped being looped into certain conversations after I disclosed. Could be coincidence. Probably wasn't.

Honestly, in my current role it's been more of a non-issue than I expected — being open has actually built trust with some colleagues. Earlier in my career, different story. I've had moments where I genuinely wondered if it cost me opportunities I just couldn't trace back.

Honestly, it's been more positive than I expected -- at least where I am now. Being open about it has actually built trust with people I work closely with, and I think it's made me a better collaborator. I'm not naive though; I've been selective about where and when I've disclosed, and I think that's part of why it hasn't cost me. Earlier in my career I kept it much closer to the chest, partly because I didn't know how it would land. That instinct wasn't wrong for that environment.

a couple of my closer coworkers already kind of knew something was up, so when I brought it up it wasn't a big deal. they were pretty chill about it — one of them actually said he'd been through something similar, which helped a lot

While flexible hours have helped me manage my anxiety, the fear of being judged still exists because of past experiences with unsupportive managers. It would be great to see more leadership training on how to handle these topics with empathy. Also, finding specialized care that is covered by standard insurance plans remains a significant challenge for many of us.

I think it's vital to recognize that mental health isn't just an internal struggle; it is often a direct response to the environments we're forced to navigate. For those of us with PTSD, workplace safety is a literal requirement, not a luxury. I hope this research leads to more robust protections for employees. honestly it is just so necessary

I appreciate that this survey brings attention to issues that are often hidden, tbh. One thing I would add is the importance of continuous feedback loops—regular, anonymous check‑ins that let employees signal emerging stress before it escalates. Also, ensuring that mental‑health resources are integrated into everyday workflows, not treated as an after‑thought its vital

One thing that wasn't quite captured here is how much informal peer support mattered alongside the formal structures -- colleagues who just knew and checked in without making it a thing. The EAP referral helped, but honestly the day-to-day stability came more from that. I'd also add that recovery while continuing to work is nonlinear; weeks that felt like progress could still be disrupted by an unexpected interaction or meeting. workplaces that can accommodate that variability, not just the initial crisis, are rare but make a real difference.

One thing the survey didn't quite have space for — the questions around disclosure and workplace response assume a fairly standard mental health context, but some situations involve a genuine safety dimension that changes the calculus entirely. My experience with PTSD wasn't just about managing symptoms at work, it came from a situation where I was afraid of a specific person in my workplace. The support I eventually got was good, but the path to it involved HR in a way that most mental health conversations don't. I think that end of the spectrum -- where mental health and physical safety overlap -- gets underrepresented in how we talk about workplace mental health policy, and it might be worth asking about separately.
I mentioned my anxiety to a couple of close colleagues and they were actually very supportive and understanding.

I have been transparent with my immediate team regarding my anxiety and PTSD recovery. Most colleagues responded with empathy, though some were initially hesitant. After I gave a public talk on the subject, several coworkers shared their own experiences with me, which helped foster a more open culture. honestly, it was pretty validating to see that shift

I approached a few teammates I trusted and explained that I was experiencing anxiety and PTSD symptoms after a threatening incident. most responded with empathy, offering to cover tasks and checking in regularly; one suggested using the company’s wellness resources, which I appreciated honestly I mean

A few coworkers already knew I dealt with anxiety -- I'd given a public talk on it, so the baseline wasn't zero. When I shared more about the PTSD specifically, reactions were mostly kind, if not always perfectly calibrated. One colleague in particular checked in on me regularly, which honestly meant more than they probably realized.

A few close colleagues knew — people I trusted enough to give some context to, mostly so they'd understand if I seemed off or needed to step away from certain situations. The reactions were mostly good, honestly. One person had their own experience with trauma and that conversation ended up being more mutual than I expected. there was one coworker who got a bit awkward about it afterward, not unkind, just visibly unsure how to act — which I understood, even if it was a little isolating for a while.

Most coworkers found out when I gave a talk on anxiety at a company event — that opened up conversations I hadn't really anticipated. The reactions were mostly supportive, and a few people came up afterward to share their own experiences, which I appreciated. One or two were clearly uncomfortable, but honestly that's pretty normal and I didn't take it personally.

A couple of close colleagues knew what had happened -- not the full picture, but enough that they understood why I was sometimes avoiding certain areas of the office. One of them had dealt with anxiety herself so she got it pretty quickly, no real explanation needed. The other was more uncertain about how to react I think, but they were kind about it and mostly just carried on normally which was actually what I needed.
My coworker told me they were dealing with burnout and taking some leave.

A colleague approached me after my talk to discuss their struggle with depression. They felt quite isolated and wanted to know how I handled the vulnerability of disclosure, honestly I think they just needed to be heard. We talked through the risks and benefits of speaking with HR, and they seemed to feel a bit more empowered afterward. it was a quiet but significant conversation

My coworker came to me after a team meeting and shared that they have been dealing with severe anxiety and occasional panic attacks following a personal incident, and they seemed relieved that I listened without judgment. tbh I told them the team will support them, suggested they speak with HR about accommodations, and promised to check in regularly, which they appreciated

One colleague came to me after my talk on anxiety -- I think hearing someone speak openly made it feel safer for them to do the same. They described feeling overwhelmed and burned out, and were worried that saying anything to management would affect how they were perceived. I mostly just listened and shared what I'd found helpful in terms of practical steps, like talking to the EAP. I don't know exactly what they did after that conversation, but they seemed a bit less alone in it, which I hope counted for something.

One colleague opened up to me after I'd shared some of what I was dealing with -- they disclosed something from their own past, a different situation but involving real fear. I could tell it cost them something to say out loud. We ended up talking for longer than I expected, honestly. I just tried to listen and not minimize it.

One coworker reached out after my talk — they mentioned they'd been managing depression for a couple of years and hadn't told anyone at work before. I mostly just listened. They weren't looking for advice, just wanted to say it out loud to someone who seemed safe to tell. I checked in with them a few times after that, nothing formal, just making sure they knew the door was open.

She brought it up quietly one afternoon, said she'd been dealing with anxiety for a few years and wanted me to know in case she ever seemed off or needed to step away from something. Honestly it felt like an act of trust more than anything -- she wasn't asking for anything specific, just wanted someone to know. I told her I appreciated her telling me and mentioned I had my own stuff going on, which is how we ended up being pretty open with each other. No big moment, just a quiet conversation that made the working relationship easier.
I didn't tell any coworkers.

I confided in a small group of coworkers about the PTSD I was navigating during that period. While those specific individuals were empathetic and provided a degree of support, the overall atmosphere was quite strained. It was difficult to manage professional expectations while my physical safety felt so precarious... honestly it was just a lot to carry

I sat down with a few former teammates after the incident and explained that I was still dealing with anxiety and PTSD symptoms. most reacted with genuine concern, saying they’d missed my presence and offering to help with any pending work, while one suggested I look into the company’s counseling service – i appreciated the support even though I wish it had come sooner.

At the previous job, I was a lot more guarded -- the environment didn't feel safe enough for that kind of openness. A couple of colleagues knew something was wrong, but I didn't have the language for PTSD yet, and honestly I wasn't sure who I could trust. The reactions I got were sympathetic, but no one felt there was much they could do

At that job I kept it pretty contained — I told one person, a colleague I'd worked closely with for a while, mostly because it explained some things about how I was managing my schedule. She was kind about it, didn't make it a big deal, which was actually what I needed at the time. I don't think I wanted more than that from coworkers then. the anxiety was real but I hadn't yet learned how to talk about it in a way that felt like it was worth the vulnerability, so I kept the circle small.

I didn't really talk to coworkers there — after the manager's reaction I pulled back pretty quickly. there was one person I was closer to who could tell something was off, and I gave a vague answer about stress, nothing specific. She was kind about it but I wasn't willing to go further in that environment. I'd learned enough to know it wasn't safe to be open there.

I was pretty guarded in that environment -- when you're not sure who's safe and the problem is coming from above, you don't really know which coworkers might loop back to management. There was one person I trusted enough to say something to, and she was sympathetic, but honestly she was also trying to keep her own head down. I dont think either of us felt like there was much we could do. Most of my other colleagues had no idea what was going on.
It hasn't really affected it.

In some ways, it has actually strengthened my professional relationships because it requires a high level of trust and clarity. However, the trauma from my previous role definitely delayed my career progression while I focused on recovery. It is a balancing act, but being open has mostly allowed me to find more supportive environments. honestly it has made me much more selective about where I work

Being identified as someone with a mental health issue has had both positive and negative impacts on my career. tbh the positive side was getting flexible scheduling and supportive chats with managers – they really helped me keep up my work. but i also felt a subtle stigma that kinda held back some advancement opportunities

It's been mixed, honestly. Being open about anxiety has created some unexpected professional connections -- the talk led to conversations I found genuinely useful, and I think being visible on the topic has made certain colleagues more comfortable coming to me. The PTSD has been harder to navigate. I've wondered at times whether disclosure affected how I was perceived for certain opportunities, though it's difficult to know for certain.

The effects have been mixed, honestly. Giving a public talk on anxiety opened some doors — conversations I might not have had otherwise, colleagues who reached out afterward in ways that felt meaningful. But there have also been moments where I sensed a disclosure had quietly shifted how someone saw me professionally, a subtle recalibration in what they assumed I could handle. I've worked to counteract that through consistent performance, and I think it's largely held — but the concern doesn't fully go away.

Mixed, honestly. In my current role being open has if anything helped — it built trust with colleagues and gave me some credibility when advocating for others. But I'm also aware it may have closed doors I can't point to directly, the kind of thing that doesn't show up in any obvious way. That previous job made clear the risk is real, and it varies a lot depending on where you land.

It's mixed, honestly. In my previous role the disclosure -- or really, just raising concerns at all -- contributed to me leaving a situation that was already untenable. That set me back professionally and I spent a while being very careful about what I said and to whom.

In my current context it's been different. I gave a talk on anxiety at a company event and it was well received, and if anything it's opened some doors -- conversations about wellbeing initiatives, being seen as someone who can speak to this stuff. I don't think it's hurt my standing. But I'm also aware that not every workplace would have reacted the same way, and I made deliberate choices about where to work partly based on that.
A manager at a different company once made a joke about someone else's depression, which made me realize it was not a safe place for me to open up.

When I reported the harassment and how it was affecting my PTSD, my supervisor initially dismissed my concerns as being "too sensitive." They suggested I focus on meeting deadlines instead of addressing the underlying safety issues, which was pretty isolating tbh. It felt like they were prioritizing the company's reputation over my actual well-being... honestly it was a low point

When I first told my manager about the PTSD symptoms after the threatening incident, she brushed it off, saying everyone has bad days and that I should just 'tough it out,' tbh. She then assigned me extra projects without adjusting my workload, and later dismissed my request for flexible hours, which left me feeling isolated and dont feel confident staying

The situation at my previous job involved a colleague whose behavior had escalated to the point where I genuinely feared for my physical safety. When I raised this with management, the response was essentially that I was probably misreading things, and I should try to address it directly with the person involved. No investigation, no interim measures -- nothing that acknowledged what I was actually describing. The suggestion to "manage better" when I was already struggling to feel safe came across as a kind of institutional shrug, and honestly it delayed me getting any real support by several months.

The one that stays with me is actually from before my current role. When the situation that led to the PTSD was still ongoing, I went to HR at that job and tried to explain that I didn't feel safe — not just stressed, but genuinely unsafe around a specific person. The response was to frame it as an interpersonal conflict and suggest mediation. I wasn't asking to mediate. I was asking to be protected. The instinct to flatten it into a "both sides" workplace dispute, rather than take seriously what I was describing, was the part that did the most damage — it made me feel like I had to prove the threat was real before anything would happen, which is a terrible position to be in when you're already frightened.

It was at a startup — high pressure, understaffed, the kind of place where admitting difficulty was implicitly coded as not being cut out for it. I'd flagged that I was struggling with anxiety in a one-on-one with my manager, kept it factual, no drama. His response was basically to redirect the conversation to deadlines within about two minutes. there was no follow-up, no offer of any resource, and the dynamic shifted after that in ways that were subtle but noticeable. I left within six months.

The situation at my previous workplace involved targeted behavior from a manager that made me genuinely fear for my safety at times. When I raised this with HR -- carefully, because I knew I was in a vulnerable position -- the response was to question whether I was interpreting things correctly. there was a suggestion I was being oversensitive. My manager was actually present in one of those early conversations, which made the whole thing collapse before it really started. Nothing was documented, nothing followed up, and I eventually left because staying felt untenable.
Provide better insurance and normalize taking mental health days.

The industry needs to move beyond surface-level wellness perks and focus on structural safety and genuine psychological well-being. Managers should receive specific training on handling trauma disclosures with empathy rather than dismissal. Normalizing these conversations through leadership transparency would also help reduce the stigma that prevents people from seeking support. it’s about building a culture of actual safety honestly

Employers should normalise mental‑health disclosures by offering clear policies, easy access to counseling, and flexible work options, and also ensure managers get training on supportive communication. It also helps when leaders model openness and provide regular check‑ins. tbh building a culture where asking for help isnt seen as a weakness could really shift things

The biggest gap I've seen is between stated policy and actual practice. Most organizations have an EAP listed somewhere, but whether a manager knows how to respond when someone actually discloses -- that's a different question entirely. More consistent training for managers, not just HR, would help. And honestly, the industry's culture around productivity and resilience still makes it harder than it should be to say "I'm not okay" without worrying it'll be held against you. the structural piece matters too: accessible, confidential support that doesn't require a crisis to trigger.

The biggest gap I've seen is between policy and actual response — most companies have an EAP listed somewhere, but what happens when someone discloses something serious depends almost entirely on the individual manager. Training managers to act rather than just listen would help a lot. And for situations involving genuine safety concerns, HR needs a clearer mandate to respond rather than mediate. the cultural conversation around mental health is improving, but the structural piece honestly hasn't caught up.

The most meaningful shift would be normalizing disclosure before someone's in crisis — making it something you can raise early rather than a last resort. Manager training matters more than most employers seem to realize, honestly. A written EAP nobody knows about doesn't help. The response to disclosure is where things succeed or fail, and that's still pretty inconsistent across the industry.

The biggest gap I've seen is managers not knowing what to do with a disclosure once it happens -- training tends to stop at "be supportive" without giving people concrete next steps. Beyond that, I think neutral reporting channels matter more than most companies admit, because if the problem involves someone's direct manager the whole structure falls apart. And honestly, just normalizing the conversation earlier would help. Not waiting for a crisis to be the first time mental health comes up.

My manager was very professional and focused on practical solutions when I shared my PTSD diagnosis. They worked with me to establish a flexible schedule for treatment and adjusted how we handle high-pressure deadlines to minimize triggers. it was a validating experience to be treated with respect... honestly it made all the difference in my recovery

After I disclosed my anxiety and PTSD to my manager, she listened carefully, asked me to specify what accommodations would help, and immediately arranged flexible working hours, a quieter workspace, and regular check‑ins with HR. tbh the team also volunteered to share workload when needed, which made me feel genuinely supported and able to stay productive, and I dont feel guilty about taking time off when needed

When I spoke to HR at my current job about the PTSD, they listened without minimizing what I was describing -- which was, honestly, already a meaningful contrast. They followed up with concrete steps: environmental adjustments and a referral to the EAP. My manager was looped in with appropriate discretion. It didn't fix everything overnight, but I felt like the institution was actually responding rather than just waiting for the problem to go away.

The response at my current job stands out by comparison. When I finally laid out the full picture — the PTSD, the reason for it, the fact that I'd needed to fear for my physical safety — my manager didn't flinch or try to reframe it. She asked what I needed, and she meant it practically: adjusted deadlines, coverage for some responsibilities while I was getting more acute support, and a standing check-in that was genuinely about how I was doing rather than just whether I was functional. HR in that instance also moved to act rather than investigate whether action was warranted. I think what made it land differently was that no one tried to normalize it or make it smaller than it was. they just took the next step.

The situation I described with HR — that one actually holds up as the example I'd point to. I'd requested the meeting expecting to have to fight for any kind of accommodation, and instead my manager came in having already talked to HR before we sat down together. They'd thought about it. The immediate ask was what I needed to feel safe, not a reassurance that the situation wasn't as serious as I was making it. Remote flexibility was arranged the same week, and there was a check-in a month later — not performative, just a genuine "how is this working." what made it feel well-handled was that nobody minimized it, and the support had actual follow-through rather than stopping at the initial conversation.

When I disclosed to HR at my current employer, the contrast with what I'd experienced before was pretty stark. I gave them enough context to explain what I needed without laying out the full history, and they took it at face value -- no pushback, no suggestion I was misreading things. They connected me with the EAP quickly and worked out a practical arrangement around workspace flexibility without making it a whole process. My manager needed a little time to find their footing, but they asked what would actually help rather than assuming, which made a real difference. I think what made it work was that the people involved treated it as a practical problem to solve rather than something to manage me around.

Q_PE.human: Once i chose to confide in a manager about my battle with major depression and recovery from addiction/alcoholism. They later threw it in my face when I decided to quit and used my past honesty to insult me.

variants.t: I never spoke to them about it.

tbh i sat down with my former manager after i told him i was dealing with severe depression and early recovery from alcoholism. he kinda nodded, but said the team couldn't afford any slowdown and told me to just take a short break, offering a single day of mental‑health leave, but no ongoing support or accommodations. honestly i left feeling pretty dismissed

the previous job was actually less dramatic about it. i didn't disclose much -- just mentioned i was dealing with some health stuff and needed to adjust my schedule temporarily. they were pretty hands-off, which i think i preferred at the time. no real conversation happened, just a nod and a schedule change. looking back i'm not sure if that was respect for my privacy or just indifference

at a previous job i didn't really say anything -- i was early in figuring out what was even going on with me, and the culture there wasn't the kind of place you'd ever bring something like that up. honestly that silence felt safer at the time. it wasn't until later that i started thinking openness might actually be okay at work. i was wrong about that too, as it turned out.

didn't go nearly as well as i hoped. i was still pretty early in figuring out the depression piece -- hadn't addressed the drinking yet -- and i mentioned to my supervisor that i was having a hard time. she sort of nodded and said to "reach out to HR if i needed resources." that was it. no follow-up, nothing changed. i don't think she knew what to do, but the silence felt like a door shutting

same situation, different job. i was more guarded that time around -- didn't get into specifics, just mentioned i was going through something personal and might need some flexibility. my manager nodded, said "of course," and then nothing changed. no follow-up, no resources mentioned. not hostile like the next job would be, just... indifferent.

Q_PC.human: I became close enough to consider some of my past coworkers friends. I was able to open up to them about medications I was taking, seeing a therapist, and the struggles I was going through. These friends were very supportive, some ended up asking for advice about getting their own therapy. It was really a relief to have people I could trust and be honest with at work, if I was feeling extra bad on some days.

variants.t: At my last company, I mostly kept my mental health issues to myself because I was worried about the stigma. I only told one close friend I was stressed, and they were very supportive but surprised.

when i told a few of my old teammates that i was dealing with depression and was in recovery, they immediately asked how i was holding up and said they'd help cover my tasks if i needed break. one of them even shared their own anxiety struggles, which made me feel less alone, though a couple seemed a bit uncomfortable about talking openly about mental health

at that job i kept it pretty close to the chest, so there wasn't much of a conversation to speak of. a couple of coworkers knew something was off -- you can't hide everything -- and one of them checked in once, asked if i was okay. i said yeah, mostly fine. she didn't push and i didn't offer more. it was kind, just... surface level

even at that earlier job there were a couple people i got close to over time, and things did come up -- not in any formal way, more just venting over drinks after work or a quiet check-in when i was clearly having a rough week. nobody had language for it really, we just kind of looked out for each other. it wasnt the deep mutual support i found later but it was something.

at that job i didn't really open up to coworkers the way i later did. i was still in denial about a lot of it, honestly. one or two people noticed i seemed off and asked if i was okay -- i gave the standard "just tired" answer and they let it go. i think if i'd been more honest they might have responded better, but i wasn't ready and the environment didn't exactly invite it

didn't really open up to coworkers at that job -- i was keeping things pretty contained there. one person i was friendly with noticed i seemed off and asked if i was okay, i just said "going through some stuff" and she left it at that. no pressure, which i appreciated. but i wasn't close enough to anyone there to let them in the way i eventually did later.
I mentioned my anxiety to my boss, and he was supportive, allowing me to start working remotely.

i told my manager i was dealing with severe depression and was in recovery from alcoholism. tbh, he listened for a few minutes, then said i should just take short break and focus on work, and later used my disclosure in a performance review to question my reliability. honestly the company offered one‑day mental‑health leave but no ongoing support

i told my manager i was struggling with depression and was in early recovery thinking it would at least explain some of what i was going through. he seemed supportive in the moment, said all the right things about flexibility. then it showed up in my performance review -- framed as concerns about reliability and commitment. that was a gut punch. i learned pretty fast that openness with management doesn't always protect you

i opened up to my manager during a really hard stretch -- i was dealing with depression and also early recovery, and i genuinely thought he was someone i could trust with that. he seemed supportive at first, said the right things. then it got used against me in ways i wont get into here, but that conversation fundamentally changed how i see authority at work.

i told my manager i was dealing with depression and that i'd just come out of treatment for alcoholism. he seemed supportive at first -- said all the right things about "working with me" and keeping it between us. then about three weeks later he brought it up in a performance review as evidence i was unreliable. no support was ever actually put in place, my disclosure just got weaponized

i told my manager i was dealing with major depression and recovering from alcoholism -- felt like the right thing, being upfront. big mistake. he used it in a performance review maybe two months later, framing me as unreliable, said my "judgment had been affected." no support was offered, no EAP mention, nothing. just a quiet shift in how he talked about me to the rest of the team after that.
I told my teammates about my anxiety. They were very understanding and didn't judge me.

I told my desk mate that I was feeling really overwhelmed and burnt out lately. She was actually very supportive and mentioned she had been seeing a therapist for similar issues. It made me feel much better knowing I wasn't the only one struggling with the pressure of our deadlines.

We were in the break room after a stressful sprint, and I mentioned feeling exhausted and anxious. One colleague nodded, saying they’d been burning out too, and suggested taking a short walk together. Another laughed nervously, then offered to share a meditation app link, promising to check in later.

I told my project manager that I was struggling with some pretty severe anxiety lately and needed to take a few mental health days to get back on track. He was actually surprisingly cool about it and told me to take whatever time I needed. He mentioned that he had gone through something similar a few years back. It made me feel a lot less alone at work.

We were sitting in the break room after a tight deadline, and I mentioned feeling constantly exhausted and anxious. One coworker nodded, saying they’d been struggling with sleep too, and offered to grab coffee together later. Another laughed nervously, then admitted they sometimes use meditation apps during lunch. A third seemed uncomfortable, muttering they didn’t think mental‑health talks belong at work, but promised to listen if I needed support.

i've talked to my close work friends about my depression and being in recovery. it was actually a really good talk. i told them i was struggling and they were super supportive. they didn't judge me at all, which meant a lot. we just talked about how hard the industry can be sometimes

i gathered a few trusted teammates after work and opened up about my depression and past addiction, explaining how my manager had weaponised my vulnerability. they listened, some nodded, one said “we’ve got your back,” another offered to check in weekly, and we all agreed to support each other moving forward

tbh, when i opened up to a few close teammates about my depression and recovery, they were genuinely concerned, asking how i was feeling and offering to cover my tickets when i needed break, and one of them even shared their own struggles, which made me feel less alone and more willing to keep talking

coworkers were a completely different story, honestly. a few of them had gone through their own stuff and were upfront about it, which made it easier to open up. one guy i worked closely with had dealt with depression too and we just kind of... started checking in on each other. it felt like actual solidarity rather than HR-speak. those friendships got me through some of the harder stretches in a way that management never could

totally different experience than with my manager. a few coworkers became people i genuinely leaned on -- they'd had their own struggles and weren't afraid to say so. there was no agenda, no power dynamic, just people looking out for each other. some of those friendships are honestly the reason i stayed in the industry as long as i did.

a few coworkers already knew about the alcoholism because we'd gotten close outside of work. when i opened up about struggling again they didn't flinch -- one of them checked in with me almost every morning for a couple months, another would just text asking if i wanted to grab lunch. honestly those friendships kept me functional in a way no formal support ever did

totally different experience than with my manager. a couple of coworkers already knew i was in recovery -- i'd told them during a rough stretch and they just... showed up. one guy in particular checked in on me regularly, brought me coffee when i was clearly struggling, never made it weird. it felt like actual friendship, not pity. that honestly kept me going more than anything the company ever did.
A coworker once shared they were feeling burnt out and depressed. I listened and suggested they talk to HR about taking some personal leave for a bit.
My desk mate opened up about her anxiety and how therapy helps her manage stress during busy weeks.
They told me they felt overwhelmed, admitted recent panic attacks, and asked if I could listen without judgment.
A close coworker told me they were feeling burnt out and depressed. Since I had just gone through my own anxiety issues, I listened and offered support while we grabbed some coffee.

They told me they’ve been feeling overwhelmed since the project kickoff, describing sleepless nights and constant worry. I listened, offered a brief break, and suggested they try the company’s counseling service.
a coworker opened up about feeling burnt out and overwhelmed. i just listened and offered some peer support
my coworker told me they felt overwhelmed, confessed recent panic attacks, and asked if i could listen when needed.

tbh, a teammate pulled me aside after a sprint and told me they’ve been battling anxiety and a recent relapse into drinking. i listened, and they said they felt isolated because the manager kept pushing them hard. i reassured them that i’d cover their tickets if needed and we talked about using company’s counseling service together

he came to me first, actually. we'd been working late together on a rough sprint and he just kind of let it out -- said he'd been on medication for a while and was worried about what would happen if anyone at work found out. i think he trusted me because i'd already hinted at my own stuff. it meant a lot that he felt safe enough to say it.

one coworker in particular came to me when they were really struggling -- anxiety, some burnout, and i think they were drinking more than they wanted to admit. they just needed someone who wouldnt make it weird or treat them differently after. i'd been open about my own stuff so i think that made it easier for them to say something. i was glad they did.

one of the people i mentioned -- the one who texted about lunch -- came to me maybe a year in and said she was really struggling with anxiety, bad enough it was affecting her sleep and her ability to focus at work. she wasn't looking for solutions, just needed to say it out loud to someone she trusted. i listened, checked in when i could. felt like the least i could do after what she'd done for me.

one of the same coworkers who'd supported me through my worst stretch came to me about a year in, said he'd been struggling with anxiety bad enough he wasn't sleeping. i think he felt safe because of what i'd shared. we ended up talking for like two hours -- it wasn't a big formal thing, just two people being honest. i was really glad he trusted me with it.
It has not really hurt my career because my current manager is very understanding.

being labeled as having a mental‑health issue has been a double‑edged sword. on the one hand, i lost a promotion when my manager used my disclosure as a reason to doubt my reliability, which was pretty demoralising. on the other hand, several teammates rallied around me, gave me flexibility and even advocated for, better policies, which helped keep me in field

it set me back at that job, honestly. whatever goodwill i'd built with management evaporated pretty fast once i put a name to what i was going through -- the performance review made that clear enough. i dont know if it cost me a specific promotion but it definitely changed how i was perceived. i'm more careful now about who i tell, even though i havent gone fully silent about it

it cost me, honestly. after that conversation with my manager things shifted -- i got passed over for a project i'd been leading up to, and i noticed the way some people treated me changed. nothing i could ever prove, nothing formally documented, just a slow erosion of trust and opportunity. it's shaped how carefully i manage what i share now, even though part of me still believes openness matters.

the performance review thing set me back pretty concretely -- i got passed over for a project lead role about six months after that, and i'm fairly certain it was connected. hard to prove, but the timing and what my manager said made it obvious. i've been more careful since about what i disclose and to who, which honestly feels like its own kind of loss

directly, yeah. that performance review where my manager weaponized my disclosure -- i didn't get the promotion i was up for that cycle. i'm pretty sure that wasn't a coincidence. and there's this low-grade thing that follows you, where you wonder if every weird interaction or being left off a project is connected. it's hard to prove but hard to ignore too.
My old boss told me to just work harder.

tbh the meeting with my manager turned into a sting. i told him i was battling severe depression and in early recovery, and he nodded but then said the team couldn't afford any slowdown, offered just a one‑day mental‑health leave, and later cited my disclosure in performance review to question my reliability. the whole thing felt like a betrayal and left me doubting staying

it was the performance review, about three months after i'd opened up to my manager. he'd been so measured and reasonable in the moment -- said he appreciated me being honest, that we'd figure it out together. then i'm sitting across from him reading comments about "inconsistent follow-through" and "questions about long-term commitment to the role." nothing was said directly, but i knew exactly what it referred to. he never even brought it up to my face.

it was the conversation i mentioned with my manager -- i told him i was dealing with depression and that i was in early recovery. he responded warmly in the moment, asked questions, said he appreciated me trusting him. then over the next few months i watched that information get quietly weaponized. framed as performance concerns, used to justify sidelining me. never overt enough to confront directly, which almost made it worse.

the performance review is the one that really sticks. i'd disclosed voluntarily, in good faith, because i thought my manager was trustworthy -- he'd been warm about it, said the right things. then three weeks later i'm sitting in a formal review with HR in the room and he's citing my depression and recovery as evidence of "inconsistency." there was nothing i could say that didn't sound defensive. i felt exposed and honestly a little stupid for trusting him

the review came out of nowhere -- i'd told him maybe eight weeks before, and things seemed fine on the surface. no warning signs. then i'm sitting across from him and he's reading from notes about "concerning judgment patterns" and "reliability concerns." i realized partway through that every example he cited mapped to the period i'd disclosed. he never said the word depression but it was obvious what he was doing.

the coworker i mentioned -- the one we'd been doing late sprints with -- handled it better than anyone. when i eventually told him more about the depression and the recovery piece, he didn't flinch or get weird about it. just said "yeah, that makes sense, i'm glad you're still here." that was it. no advice, no pivoting to solutions. just acknowledgment. honestly that meant more to me than any formal accommodation ever did

the coworker stuff i already mentioned -- that was the well-handled version, honestly. no official process, no HR involved, just people who actually knew me and showed up. the morning check-ins, the lunch texts. it didn't fix anything structural but it kept me tethered. what made it work was that nobody made it weird or treated me like i was suddenly fragile. they just kept being my friends

tbh after i finally opened up about my depression a few teammates actually reshuffled the sprint so i could take a lighter load and a senior offered to buddy‑up with me for weekly check‑ins. the company later set up confidential counseling service and gave me flexible hours, which honestly made a big difference

the biggest thing would be actual accountability when a manager uses a disclosure against you. there's no real consequence for that right now -- you can have all the EAP programs in the world and it doesnt matter if the culture punishes honesty. and i'd push for more peer-based support structures, not just top-down resources. in my experience the coworkers were the ones who actually helped. that should be recognized and built on, not just left to chance

the biggest thing would be actual confidentiality protections -- legal ones, with real teeth for managers who weaponize disclosures in reviews. beyond that, i think companies overinvest in EAP programs nobody uses and underinvest in just letting people be actual humans with each other. the peer support that helped me wasn't a program, it was people. culture has to come first or none of the formal stuff matters

i think the biggest gap is that many companies treat mental health as a checkbox instead of a lived reality. when my manager weaponized my disclosure, it showed how power dynamics can silence people. i’ve seen colleagues thrive, when they're given real flexibility, peer support, and clear, confidential resources. i hope future workplaces build trust, not just policies

i guess the thing i keep coming back to is that the informal stuff -- the friendships, the quiet check-ins, the coworker who just said "i'm glad you're still here" -- that's what actually held me together. surveys like this tend to focus on policy and i get why, but the gap between what's written in an employee handbook and what actually happens in a one-on-one with your manager is enormous. i hope that gap is what you're trying to close

i guess i just want to say that the peer relationships i found in tech -- genuinely, unexpectedly -- are the thing that kept me going through some really dark years. the system failed me in ways that still sting, but the people didn't. i think that distinction gets lost when we talk about "workplace mental health" as a policy issue. sometimes its just about whether the person next to you gives a damn.
just that the peer thing can't be faked. you can't program it into a policy
just that the peer support piece genuinely saved me in a way no company policy ever has. i hope researchers actually look at that side of it, not just the bad management stories.
